messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 48

Mr. Harrison is a 67-year-old high school principal. He has led his school for nearly two decades, known for his steady hand and calm, measured demeanor. That reputation ended on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection two blocks from the school.

He remembers the sound first—a sound he cannot describe to anyone without his voice catching. Then the sensation of spinning, his car folding around him. He remembers the windshield fracturing into a web of white lines, and the smell of gasoline. He remembers thinking, *This is it. This is how I die.* A paramedic later told him he was trapped for twenty minutes. He does not remember that. He remembers the face of a young woman outside the shattered window, crying, and the way her voice seemed to come from very far away.

Physically, he walked away with a broken collarbone and two cracked ribs. He was discharged from the hospital the next day. But something else had broken.

At first he told himself he was fine. He returned to work less than a week later, against his wife’s protests. But now, four months on, he is not fine. He no longer drives. He cannot even sit in the passenger seat without his palms sweating and his chest tightening. His wife drives him to school every morning, and he grips the door handle the entire way, scanning every intersection as if the pickup truck is hiding behind each one. His commute—once a five-minute drive—has become a daily ordeal.

At work, he has become someone the staff do not recognize. The calm has been replaced by a short fuse. A student’s minor disruption that he would have handled with a quiet word now sends him into a silent, white-knuckled fury. He has snapped at his secretary twice this week over misplaced paperwork. After each outburst, he feels a wave of shame, then a desperate need to be alone. He has started closing his office door—something he never did—and eating lunch in there, avoiding the faculty lounge because the chatter feels overwhelming, like noise with no meaning.

Sleep is a battleground. He lies awake for hours, his mind replaying the crash in fragments: the flash of red light, the screech of tires, the sensation of the steering column against his ribs. When he does drift off, he is back in the car, trapped, with the smell of gasoline thick in his throat. He jolts awake in a cold sweat, convinced he is about to die. His wife says he moans in his sleep now. He tells her it’s nothing.

The hardest part is the way the world feels wrong. He used to love the Friday afternoon buzz of the corridors before a holiday. Now he feels like he is watching his life from behind a pane of glass. Students wave, teachers smile, but none of it feels real. He finds himself unreachable, distant, as if the person who was that principal died in the crash and someone else came back. He has stopped reading the news because every story about a car accident sends him into a spiral. He checked his PCL-5 score with his family doctor—48—and the doctor said it was high, but Mr. Harrison already knew. He feels it in each skipped heartbeat at a honk in traffic, each time he flinches when a car passes too close to the school’s front walk, each time he looks at his wife and realizes he cannot tell her what is really going on inside his head.

He has not told anyone at work about the nightmares. He is the principal. He is supposed to hold everything together. But he is beginning to wonder if the thing that broke in that intersection can ever be fixed.
